title: Fewer wants
tomorrow: the Buddha gave Anuruddha an eighth thought. what was it?

lines: THE EMPTY APARTMENT, THE FULL CART.
THIS TEACHING IS FOR ONE WHO WANTS LITTLE.
cards: Somewhere tonight, someone is watching a video of a bright, empty apartment and adding a new set of storage boxes to a cart. Wanting less can quietly become one more thing to want. An old monk met the same knot.

Anuruddha is sitting alone in a bamboo park, far from his teacher, and a thought arrives: this teaching is for one who wants little, not for one who wants much. Six more thoughts follow it, each one clear.
And then, the sutta says, quick as a strong man bends his arm, the Buddha is standing in front of him.

teach.b: Good, good, Anuruddha, he says. These are the thoughts of a great person. Then he unpacks the first one, few wants, and the unpacking has a twist.

teach.h: DON'T EVEN WANT TO LOOK SIMPLE.
teach.b: Someone of few wants, he says, doesn't even want people to know that they want little. Read that twice.

You can want a smaller life and still be wanting something: to be seen as the simple one, the calm one, the one who needs nothing. The Buddha closes that door too. The Pali word is appicchatā, wanting little.
Beside it in the sutta sits contentment: a monk content with whatever robe, whatever food, whatever shelter, whatever medicine comes.
Not content with nothing. Content with enough. That's what makes this a Buddhist teaching and not a decluttering tip.
In the first sermon, craving is named as the source of suffering. Fewer things clears a room.
Fewer wants clears the mind that keeps filling rooms.
So Buddhists practice it small: a monk eats what is put in the bowl, and on holy days some lay people keep extra precepts and go without a comfort or two. And Anuruddha?
The sutta says he went back to his solitude, practiced, and became one of the awakened. But before he went, the Buddha handed him one more thought, an eighth, that he hadn't thought of.

how: Monks practice contentment with whatever robes, food, lodging and medicine are given; on holy days some lay Buddhists keep extra precepts and give up a comfort for the day.

o: wanting little, without wanting to look simple
giving up every wish until none are left
owning as few things as you can manage

games.q: inside Anuruddha's thought — tap the pairs.

s: wanting less means wanting nothing at all
the sutta pairs few wants with contentment: content with enough, not with nothing.
the sutta warns against wanting to be known for wanting little
someone of few wants doesn't even want people to know they want little.
few wants is mostly about owning fewer things
things are the surface; the sutta goes after the wanting, even the wish to look simple.

games.q: your friend gives away half her closet and posts about it every day for a week. what would the Buddha's unpacking of few wants notice first?
o: the posting: wanting to be seen as simple is still a want.
the closet: she should give away the other half too.
nothing: giving things away is always few wants.
games.why: the Buddha told Anuruddha that someone of few wants doesn't even want to be known for it. the want can move from the closet to the feed.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting this week: a pair of shoes, a reply, a bit of praise. Hold it in mind through the sit without buying, checking or deciding anything.
Just notice the pull, where it sits in the body, and how it changes when nothing feeds it.

wordCard.voice: Fewer wants: appicchatā in Pali, wanting little, without even wanting to look like someone who wants little.

orig.note: Pali: wanting little, the first of Anuruddha's thoughts.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: few wants, and content with enough. Forty days into a life of practice.
